title: Investigating Photosynthesis Review Test
description: Use controlled comparisons, matter models, and rate data to investigate photosynthesis and distinguish oxygen production from net change.

questions.prompt: An algae model labels carbon dioxide 'energy' and sunlight 'matter.' What correction is needed?
questions.questionText: An algae model labels carbon dioxide 'energy' and sunlight 'matter.' What correction is needed?
options: Both labels should say matter.
Both labels should say oxygen.
The labels are correct because light contains carbon.
Carbon dioxide supplies matter; sunlight supplies energy.
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon dioxide supplies matter; sunlight supplies energy.
questions.explanation: Matter and energy play different roles in photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: A leafy shoot remains alive overnight. Which process can release usable energy from its stored sugars?
questions.questionText: A leafy shoot remains alive overnight. Which process can release usable energy from its stored sugars?
options: Photosynthesis without light.
Cellular respiration.
Transpiration alone.
Absorption of soil minerals alone.
questions.explanation: Respiration can use stored sugars during darkness.

questions.prompt: A sample produces 45 bubbles in five minutes. What rate was counted?
questions.questionText: A sample produces 45 bubbles in five minutes. What rate was counted?
options: 40 bubbles per minute.
9 bubbles per minute.
225 bubbles per minute.
5 bubbles per minute.
questions.explanation: 45 divided by 5 is 9; this is a count rate, not a calibrated gas volume.

questions.prompt: Which question could a controlled light-level experiment answer most directly?
questions.questionText: Which question could a controlled light-level experiment answer most directly?
options: How does the tested light change affect a measured photosynthesis proxy under matched conditions?
Do all plants in every habitat respond identically?
Does photosynthesis create carbon atoms?
Can one trial prove that nutrients never matter?
questions.correctAnswer: How does the tested light change affect a measured photosynthesis proxy under matched conditions?
questions.explanation: A controlled experiment answers a specific, bounded comparison.

questions.prompt: Two trials count equal numbers of bubbles but do not record their sizes. What extra measurement would improve comparison of released gas?
questions.questionText: Two trials count equal numbers of bubbles but do not record their sizes. What extra measurement would improve comparison of released gas?
options: The color of the experiment labels.
The total number of notebook pages.
Gas volume over the same time interval.
The age of the room's door.
questions.correctAnswer: Gas volume over the same time interval.
questions.explanation: Gas volume provides information that counts alone cannot supply.

questions.prompt: A simplified light-period model makes 13 oxygen units and uses 5. What change should the oxygen store show?
questions.questionText: A simplified light-period model makes 13 oxygen units and uses 5. What change should the oxygen store show?
options: An increase of 8 units.
An increase of 18 units.
A decrease of 5 units.
No change because both processes occur.

questions.prompt: Why does a larger oxygen gain not automatically mean a larger photosynthesis rate when comparing two different plants?
questions.questionText: Why does a larger oxygen gain not automatically mean a larger photosynthesis rate when comparing two different plants?
options: Oxygen cannot be measured in plants.
Respiration is always exactly the same in every plant.
Photosynthesis never produces oxygen.
Different respiration rates or background exchanges can affect net gain.
questions.correctAnswer: Different respiration rates or background exchanges can affect net gain.
questions.explanation: Net gain combines production and consumption and may include other exchanges.

questions.prompt: A seedling becomes taller in shade but gains less dry mass than a matched seedling in moderate light. Which interpretation fits both observations?
questions.questionText: A seedling becomes taller in shade but gains less dry mass than a matched seedling in moderate light. Which interpretation fits both observations?
options: The shaded plant must have made more sugar because it is taller.
Greater height does not necessarily mean greater accumulation of plant material.
Dry mass consists only of water.
The two observations cannot occur together.
questions.correctAnswer: Greater height does not necessarily mean greater accumulation of plant material.
questions.explanation: Shape and accumulated dry matter are different measurements.

questions.prompt: At fixed light, rates at low, medium, and high carbon dioxide are 3, 7, and 7 units. What does the plateau justify?
questions.questionText: At fixed light, rates at low, medium, and high carbon dioxide are 3, 7, and 7 units. What does the plateau justify?
options: Concluding carbon dioxide has no role in photosynthesis.
Concluding all plants have a maximum rate of 7 units.
Investigating another limiting factor rather than assuming more carbon dioxide will keep helping.
Removing the medium treatment from the data.
questions.correctAnswer: Investigating another limiting factor rather than assuming more carbon dioxide will keep helping.
questions.explanation: A plateau is a clue for a follow-up, not proof of a particular cause.

questions.prompt: A student's diagram removes respiration whenever a light arrow appears. How should it change?
questions.questionText: A student's diagram removes respiration whenever a light arrow appears. How should it change?
options: Keep respiration in the light model as well as the dark model.
Remove respiration from both models.
Show respiration only in dead leaves.
Replace water transport with respiration.
questions.correctAnswer: Keep respiration in the light model as well as the dark model.
questions.explanation: Living plant cells continue to respire in the light.

questions.prompt: One sample gains 18 oxygen units in three hours and another gains 16 in two hours. Which has the greater average net gain rate?
questions.questionText: One sample gains 18 oxygen units in three hours and another gains 16 in two hours. Which has the greater average net gain rate?
options: The first: 18 rather than 16 units per hour.
Both: 6 units per hour.
The second: 8 rather than 6 units per hour.
The second: 32 rather than 54 units per hour.
questions.correctAnswer: The second: 8 rather than 6 units per hour.
questions.explanation: Normalize the changes by duration before comparing rates.

questions.prompt: A dim-light sample has a net oxygen change of zero. Which additional evidence would distinguish 'no production' from 'production balanced by use'?
questions.questionText: A dim-light sample has a net oxygen change of zero. Which additional evidence would distinguish 'no production' from 'production balanced by use'?
options: A second label on the same container.
The leaf's shape alone.
A rule that zero net change means no reactions.
An independent estimate of oxygen consumption under comparable conditions.
questions.correctAnswer: An independent estimate of oxygen consumption under comparable conditions.
questions.explanation: Separating opposing processes needs information beyond their combined net effect.

questions.prompt: A team moves a lamp closer but uses a cooling arrangement to keep temperature steady. Why does that improve the test?
questions.questionText: A team moves a lamp closer but uses a cooling arrangement to keep temperature steady. Why does that improve the test?
options: It guarantees bubble sizes cannot change.
It reduces heating as an alternative explanation for a light-treatment effect.
It makes plant size irrelevant.
It proves carbon dioxide is unlimited.
questions.correctAnswer: It reduces heating as an alternative explanation for a light-treatment effect.
questions.explanation: Controlling one confound improves interpretation without eliminating every limitation.

questions.prompt: A light trial gains 4 oxygen units per hour; comparable respiration is estimated at 3 units per hour. With no other exchanges, what production is implied?
questions.questionText: A light trial gains 4 oxygen units per hour; comparable respiration is estimated at 3 units per hour. With no other exchanges, what production is implied?
options: 7 oxygen units per hour.
1 oxygen unit per hour.
4 oxygen units per hour.
12 oxygen units per hour.
questions.explanation: Production must replace the 3 used and supply the 4 net gain: 7.

questions.prompt: A drought-stressed plant receives bright light but has mostly closed stomata. Which prediction best connects water balance and photosynthesis?
questions.questionText: A drought-stressed plant receives bright light but has mostly closed stomata. Which prediction best connects water balance and photosynthesis?
options: Bright light guarantees maximum sugar production regardless of gas entry.
Stomatal closure supplies extra carbon dioxide to every cell.
Reduced carbon dioxide entry may limit sugar production despite abundant light.
Water balance and photosynthesis cannot affect each other.
questions.correctAnswer: Reduced carbon dioxide entry may limit sugar production despite abundant light.
questions.explanation: Water-saving responses can constrain a matter input needed for photosynthesis.
